title: DNS cache coherence & invalidation playbook (draft)
body:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for handling DNS cache coherence and controlled invalidation across hybrid Redwood Private deployments (VPC + on-prem). Focus: reduce stale resolution windows, avoid long tail latency due to cached negative records, and provide Terraform module notes for automating safe TTL changes and rollbacks.

Context / problem statement:
- Private deployments use a mix of cloud private zones (Route53 / Cloud DNS), on-prem BIND clusters, and lightweight local caches (dnsmasq/systemd-resolved) running as node-level forwarders.
- We recently observed incidents where a certificate rotation + service IP change resulted in 11–17 minute windows of 5xx across customer pods because DNS TTLs and downstream caches didn’t expire coherently.
- Goal: provide operational patterns for (1) proactive TTL changes, (2) immediate invalidation paths when needed, and (3) Terraform-managed DNS forwarding/zone modules that include safe knobs.

High-level approach / principles:
- Default TTL hygiene: use conservative low TTLs for service endpoints we expect to change during deploys (30–60s). Use longer TTLs for stable infra (5–15m).
- Avoid mechanical TTL slashing as a permanent strategy; treat low TTLs as an explicit deploy-time setting, then increase after rollouts succeed.
- Provide a controlled invalidation path: a coordination API that (a) publishes a short-lived override zone, and (b) schedules Terraform updates to authoritative zone records.
- Instrument cache-hit metrics at the forwarder layer and alert on negative cache growth / NXDOMAIN spikes.

Terraform module notes (proposed modules):
- module: tf-private-dns-zone (authoritative zone provisioning)
  - variables: zone_name, providers (cloud, onprem), record_sets as map, ttl_default
  - outputs: zone_id, last_change_id
  - safe operations: apply with target-record for rollout, create a "staged-record" resource used for cutover, separate plan/apply for cutover to avoid accidental mass overwrite

- module: tf-dns-forwarder (edge forwarders / cache hosts)
  - variables: forwarders (list), resolver_mode (systemd|dnsmasq|unbound), cache_ttl_min, cache_ttl_max, healthcheck_port
  - notes: forwarders are configured with a plugin that can accept an "invalidate" webhook. We provision an ingress ACL for that webhook in the private control plane.

- module: tf-split-horizon-automation
  - purpose: create split-horizon forwarding rules (cloud -> internal zone, onprem -> stub zone) + consistent ACLs across regions
  - pattern: keep a small number of canonical forwarders per region and publish their IPs to the zone modules.

Operational runbook (fast invalidation use-case):
1) Detect problem: perf dashboard shows DNS p95 > 200ms and spike in 5xx for service X. Check forwarder metrics and pod resolv.conf.
2) Verify authoritative record change: confirm new A / CNAME exists in authoritative zone (Confluence link). If missing, fix authoritative zone via tf-private-dns-zone staged-record apply (manual plan review required).
3) If authoritative is correct but stale caches persist, trigger invalidation: POST to /invalidate on canonical region-forwarder (IP list in tf-dns-forwarder output). The webhook instructs forwarders to purge specific name and clears negative cache for that qtype.
4) If webhook not available (older clusters), fallback: rotate forwarder IPs via tf-dns-forwarder (provision new forwarder, then update zone to point at new forwarder IPs) — higher-impact, longer route but effective.
5) After invalidation, monitor: DNS cache hit rate, resolution latency p50/p95, service 5xx rate. Typical target: resolve success < 5s after invalidation, and p95 DNS < 50ms.
6) Once stable, revert any temporary low TTLs back to standard values via tf-private-dns-zone.

Testing and verification:
- Unit tests: terraform plan outputs for staged-record creation must not delete existing records by default. Add guards in CI that refuse plans where more than N records would be removed.
- Integration tests: from a bastion host in each region and on-prem, run: dig +noedns +norecurse @<forwarder> <name> A; dig +trace <name>; verify TTL observed matches expected.
- Chaos test: where safe, run a scripted authority switch: create staged-record, wait for caches to warm, then cutover while measuring app error rate and DNS resolution times.

Metrics & alerts to add (Grafana/Prometheus):
- forwarder_dns_request_rate (by qtype)
- forwarder_cache_hit_ratio (p90 target > 0.8)
- forwarder_negative_cache_rate (alert if sustained rise > 3x baseline)
- dns_resolution_latency_seconds (p50/p95) per region
- zone_change_failures (terraform apply errors)
Alert thresholds: immediate paging if forwarder_negative_cache_rate > 0.1rps per node for 5m AND service 5xx increase > 1%.

Safe rollback patterns:
- Never delete canonical records in bulk during a remediation window. Use staged-record + cutover.
- If a forced rollback is required, revert authoritative record to previous value and trigger invalidation. If invalidation webhook unavailable, perform forwarder rotation.
- Keep a one-click rollback dashboard that runs a pre-approved tf apply for the last-known-good staged-record.

Edge cases & pitfalls we've observed:
- DNS negative caching (NXDOMAIN) TTLs often longer than positive records; remember to consider SOA minimum-ttl and negative-ttl settings in BIND and cloud providers.
- systemd-resolved and node-level caching layers sometimes ignore EDNS; tests must include EDNS and fragmented responses.
- HTTP clients with aggressive connection pools can mask DNS propagation issues (they hold old IPs). Include a client-side socket-level drain step in rollout playbook.

Notes on NAT / Egress interplay:
- Changing forwarder IPs can affect NAT session affinity for outbound flows. If forwarder IP rotates without updating NAT tables, return traffic may be blackholed for clients behind stateful NAT (applies to some on-prem appliances).
- When rotating forwarder IPs, coordinate with SRE to flush NAT sessions or schedule in maintenance window.

Rollout checklist (pre-deploy):
- [ ] Identify records that will change and mark TTLs to 30–60s for < 10m pre-deploy
- [ ] Open ticket (INFRA-2419) with list of affected zones and owners
- [ ] Create staged-record in tf-private-dns-zone and run plan + human review
- [ ] Ensure invalidation webhook endpoint is healthy (tf-dns-forwarder outputs)
- [ ] Smoke test from 3 vantage points (cloud A, cloud B, onprem)

Quick commands (notes to operator):
- Check cache on forwarder: systemd-resolve --statistics; nslookup <name> <forwarder_ip>
- Purge via webhook: curl -X POST https://<forwarder_ip>:<port>/invalidate -d '{"name":"svc.example.internal","type":"A"}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
- Rotate forwarder (terraform): cd infra/dns-forwarder && terraform apply -var='rotate=true' -target=module.new_forwarder

Open questions / TODOs:
- Add an endpoint in the control plane UI to run invalidations (auth + audit trail) — design ticket needed.
- Can we standardize a small shim binary for forwarders that exposes metrics + invalidate API across systemd-resolved/dnsmasq/unbound? (Ravi TODO)
- Document provider-specific negative TTL semantics (AWS vs GCP vs BIND) and keep as a short table in Confluence.

Attachments and references:
- GitHub PR for forwarder webhook: https://github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules/pull/142
- Incident notes: CONFLUENCE-1234-dns-cache-playbook
- Jira: INFRA-2419 (rollout guardrail for TTL changes)

Notes to self: rough, can split into separate templates: 1) quick-invalidation playbook, 2) terraform module pattern doc, 3) control-plane UI proposal. Keep this file as the single source of operational steps until we refactor.
